proof_summary: For an arbitrary bound \(B\), apply the hypothesis at \(n=(6(B+1)+1)!/6\) to obtain \(n=x+y\) with the required primes and the identity \((6(B+1)+1)!=(6x-1)+(6y+1)\). If either \(6x-1\) or the lower twin prime \(6y-1\) were at most \(6(B+1)\), then respectively \(6x-1\) or \(6y+1\) would divide the factorial and hence the prime on the other side of the identity, forcing it to be \(1\) or equal to that prime; positivity and their incompatible residues modulo \(6\) rule this out, so both prime families are unbounded and therefore infinite.
